title: How Casinos Really Make Money (It's Not Just Gambling)
summary: Roulette's house edge is 5.26%, yet Nevada's roulette tables kept 19% in 2025, and at MGM's Las Vegas Strip resorts the casino brought in only 24% of revenue. Here's how the edge, money played again and again, and the rest of the building make the house win. This video explains a business; it is not gambling advice.

hooks.hook: At MGM's resorts on the Las Vegas Strip, gambling brought in less than a quarter of the money last year.
In 1964, Las Vegas changed the rules of blackjack, then had to change them back.
Roulette's house edge is 5%. Nevada's roulette tables kept 19%.
Nevada casinos won a record $15.8 billion in 2025, and two thirds came from slot machines.
If the odds are only a few percent, how does the house always win?

Our math: slots share of Nevada win 10,713.8 / 15,798.5 = 67.8%; MGM Strip casino share 2,013.7 / 8,441.5 = 23.9%; $100 x 5.26% = about $5.

scenes.narration: At MGM's resorts on the Las Vegas Strip, gambling brought in less than a quarter of the money last year. So how does the house always win?
The story starts in {1962,|nineteen sixty-two,} when a mathematician named Edward Thorp published a book on how to beat blackjack by counting cards. It sold over a million copies.

So in {1964,|nineteen sixty-four,} Nevada's big resort hotels changed the rules of blackjack. Then people stopped playing, and the casinos changed the rules back. Why give up their own protection? Hold that thought.
Casinos win in three ways: a small edge, the same money played again and again, and everything else in the building. Let's open the books.
Part one. The small edge.
Take roulette. An American wheel has {38|thirty-eight} pockets: one to {36,|thirty-six,} plus a zero and a double zero.
Those two green pockets give the house an edge of {5.26 percent|five point two six percent} on almost every bet.
So for every hundred dollars bet, the math says the casino keeps about five. That sounds small.
But in {2025,|twenty twenty-five,} Nevada's roulette tables kept {19 percent|nineteen percent} of the money players changed into chips.
How does five become nineteen? Not better odds. The same chips, bet again and again.
Win a little, bet it again. Lose a little, bet again. Every spin takes its cut of whatever is still on the table, until the chips run out.
If you like seeing the receipts behind everyday prices, subscribe. New ones every Tuesday and Friday.
Part two. The quiet machine.
In {2025,|twenty twenty-five,} Nevada's casinos won a record {$15.8 billion|fifteen point eight billion dollars} from gamblers.
And about two thirds of it came from slot machines, not the card tables you see in the movies.

scenes.narration: Slots kept about seven cents of every dollar played through them. No dealer to pay, and no cards to count.
But gambling is only part of the bill. Remember MGM's quarter? Here's where the rest comes from.
Part three. The rest of the building.

Here's MGM on the Strip in {2025.|twenty twenty-five.} The casino brought in {$2 billion.|two billion dollars.} Rooms, {$2.9 billion.|two point nine billion.} Food and drink, {$2.3 billion,|two point three billion,} and shows and shops another {$1.3 billion.|one point three billion.}

scenes.narration: So the casino floor isn't the whole business. It brings in the crowd, and the building sells that crowd everything else.

And to keep that crowd, casinos give a lot away. In Clark County, home of Las Vegas, casinos handed out about {$3.8 billion|three point eight billion dollars} in free rooms, food and drinks in one year.
About four in every ten dollars of drinks they served were on the house. That isn't generosity. It's the cost of keeping you at the table.

Now, back to {1964.|nineteen sixty-four.} Why did the casinos give in? Because when blackjack got worse, players walked away. And a player who walks away takes the rooms, the dinners and the drinks with them.
That's the real house edge. Not one lucky game, but time: keeping you inside, playing the same chips again and again.
And it's working. A record {$78.7 billion|seventy-eight point seven billion dollars} went to America's commercial casinos and betting apps in {2025.|twenty twenty-five.}
The house doesn't need luck. It needs your time. Next time: why car washes would rather sell you a membership than a wash.
